text: The office smelled like cold coffee and old regrets, which was about right for the rent I paid. I had a desk, a bottle in the bottom drawer, and a window that looked out on a city that never bothered to look back. The fan turned slow circles over my head like a vulture that had decided I wasn't dead enough yet. It was a Tuesday, and Tuesdays in Los Angeles have a way of going bad faster than milk in August. I lit a cigarette and watched the smoke crawl up toward the ceiling stain shaped like a state I'd never wanted to visit. Down on the street a bus groaned past, hauling its cargo of the tired and the broke to wherever the tired and the broke get hauled. My phone sat there saying nothing, the way it had said nothing for three days, the way a dead man says nothing when you ask him who pulled the trigger. I poured two fingers of rye and told myself it was medicinal. The bottle didn't argue. Nothing in that office ever argued with me except the calendar, and the calendar was winning. I was forty dollars from honest work and a thousand miles from anything that resembled luck. Somewhere out there a client was making up his mind to lie to me. I could feel it coming on, the way old men feel rain.

She came in out of the rain like the rain had personally apologized and sent her ahead as a peace offering. The kind of blonde that makes a bishop kick a hole in a stained-glass window. She had a face you'd remember in your sleep and regret in the morning, and a coat that probably cost more than my car, my office, and whatever was left of my self-respect combined. Water dripped off her hat brim and pooled on my floor, and I didn't tell her to stop. There are some things a man doesn't interrupt. She sat without being asked, crossed a pair of legs that had clearly been to finishing school, and looked at me like I was a stain she'd hire someone else to remove. 'They tell me you're discreet,' she said. Her voice was low and smooth and carried just enough trouble in it to fill a hearse. 'They tell me a lot of things,' I said. 'Most of them aren't true and the rest are worse.' She smiled, and it was a beautiful smile, the kind they bury you in. Outside, the neon from the chop suey joint across the street bled red across her cheek, and for a second she looked like exactly what she was, which was the most expensive kind of bad news a man could buy.

The rain came down on Bunker Hill like the sky had finally run out of patience with the whole rotten town. It hammered the tin awnings and ran black in the gutters and turned the streetlights into smeared yellow smudges that didn't light anything so much as remind you how dark it was. I had my collar up and my hat down and a feeling in my gut like I'd swallowed a brick and it wanted out. The address I wanted was a rooming house that had given up on dignity around the time Coolidge gave up on the presidency. The kind of place where the wallpaper hangs on out of habit and the stairs creak the names of everybody who ever climbed them broke and climbed down broker. I went up two flights past a smell of boiled cabbage and human surrender. A radio behind one door was playing something with strings that wanted to be sad and only managed tired. At the top a single bulb swung on its cord like a man who hadn't quite finished hanging himself. Door number nine had a crack of light under it and a quiet behind it that was too quiet, the kind of quiet that has a body in it somewhere. I reached for the knob and the gun in my coat felt suddenly heavy and useless, the way a prayer feels when you've forgotten the words.

My client had a smile like a cracked sidewalk and a handshake that felt like shaking hands with a wet trout. He wore a suit that cost real money and a conscience that had clearly come secondhand. The first thing he did was lie to me, and he did it so smoothly I almost respected him for it. Said the missing girl was his secretary. The way he said secretary, you could hear the quotation marks fall off the end and roll across my floor. He slid a photograph across the desk along with a check, and the check had more zeroes than the story had truth, which is generally how you know a story has none at all. 'Just find her,' he said. 'Quietly.' Quietly is what they always want, the men with too much money and too little spine. It means find her but don't find anything else, don't lift any rocks, don't notice what's under them wriggling. I looked at the check, then at his face, then at the rain doing slow work on the window. A man can talk himself into a lot of things when his bank account is wheezing. I picked up the check and felt about as clean as a parking-lot puddle. 'I'll find her,' I said. He smiled that cracked-sidewalk smile again, and somewhere a long way off, my better judgment quietly packed a bag and left town.

Three in the morning is the hour the city takes its mask off, and what's underneath isn't pretty and never apologizes. I was parked across from a nightclub that called itself the Flamingo, though the only thing pink about it was the bruise it would leave on your wallet. The neon bird out front flickered like it was trying to remember how to fly and had decided against it. Inside, somewhere, a saxophone was working overtime on a tune nobody had asked it to play. I'd been sitting in that car so long my legs had filed a grievance and the windshield had fogged into something a man could write his last will on. A black sedan slid up to the curb, smooth and patient as a hearse with somewhere to be. Two men got out. They had the shoulders of men who broke things for a living and the faces of men who'd stopped charging extra for it. One of them looked up and down the street the way a butcher looks at a side of beef. I sank lower in my seat and breathed shallow and thought about all the honest professions I could have picked instead of this one. Accounting. Plumbing. Anything where the worst thing waiting in the dark was a bad number. The men went inside. The saxophone kept playing, and the night kept its mouth shut, the way the night always does right before everything goes wrong.
